paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders try to turn a language model’s internal activations into a collection of interpretable features. But an appealing interpretation is difficult to verify when researchers do not know the model’s underlying concepts. This paper asks a practical question: do those features help predict concepts from activations better than established alternatives?

The authors test activation probing under four challenging conditions: limited training data, uneven class frequencies, noisy labels, and changes in the input distribution. Their hypothesis is that concept-like features could provide useful structure when learning from difficult data. Although sparse autoencoders sometimes improve results on individual datasets, ensembles incorporating them do not consistently beat ensembles built entirely from baseline methods.

The authors also examine identifying misleading correlations, detecting poor dataset quality, and probing across multiple tokens. Simple alternatives achieve similar results in these settings. The findings therefore challenge the demonstrated practical advantage of current sparse autoencoders for these tasks, while leaving their usefulness elsewhere open. They also show why strong downstream comparisons matter when evaluating interpretability methods.
icml-2025-are-sparse-autoencoders-useful.tldr: Sparse autoencoders offer occasional probing gains, but the tested combinations do not consistently outperform strong alternatives without them.

paragraphs: When a prediction system can consult both classifiers and human experts, each additional human opinion has a cost. This paper studies how to maintain accurate class predictions while asking fewer questions. It combines probability estimates from pretrained classifiers with a Bayesian model of the labels that experts would provide.

A central feature is that the framework represents correlations among experts through shared hidden variables. This lets it reason jointly about their opinions instead of treating every response as unrelated evidence. Using simulations, the system estimates how useful another expert query would be. It also maintains probability distributions over the responses of experts who have not yet been consulted.

The authors evaluate the approach on two medical classification problems and on CIFAR-10H and ImageNet-16H. They report substantially lower human-query costs than the compared baselines while maintaining high prediction accuracy. The practical contribution is a framework for deciding when further consultation is valuable, using both the classifier’s uncertainty and relationships among human judgments.
icml-2025-bayesian-inference-for-correla.tldr: A Bayesian framework models correlated expert opinions to reduce human queries while maintaining high classification accuracy in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for a good action while limiting expensive evaluations. Here, each evaluation reveals only which of two actions a person prefers, rather than a numerical score. The paper asks how efficiently a learner can find a nearly optimal action from this reduced form of feedback.

The analysis uses the Bradley-Terry-Luce preference model, the same framework adopted by the prior work being improved. The authors derive tighter regret bounds whose leading dependence is the square root of the number of queries multiplied by maximum information gain, apart from suppressed logarithmic factors. Information gain captures a complexity contribution determined by the kernel used to model the objective.

For common kernels, these guarantees recover the order-optimal sample complexity available to conventional Bayesian optimization with richer feedback. Thus, under the analyzed framework, preference comparisons can suffice at the same sample-complexity order as numerical evaluations. This matters when people can supply comparisons but obtaining many judgments is costly: reduced feedback need not impose a worse theoretical query rate in these settings.
icml-2025-bayesian-optimization-from-hum.tldr: Under a standard preference model, tighter guarantees show that comparisons can match numerical feedback’s optimal sample-complexity order for common kernels.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning estimates a distribution of returns rather than only an average return. This paper studies categorical representations, which express that distribution through probabilities over a collection of outcomes, trained using a Kullback-Leibler divergence loss. Earlier theoretical work instead used a Cramér-distance loss, leaving a gap between the analyzed objective and the one of interest here.

The authors introduce a preconditioned version of the algorithm and prove its convergence. They also derive the asymptotic variance of its categorical estimates under different learning-rate regimes. This characterizes the estimates’ remaining statistical variability in the long run and enables a comparison with classical reinforcement learning, extending the analysis beyond whether the algorithm eventually converges.

Experiments validate the theoretical findings and investigate the relative strengths of KL-based losses. The paper also derives practical guidance from that investigation. Its main contribution is to connect convergence and long-run statistical behavior to a KL-trained categorical method, giving both a theoretical foundation for the proposed modification and empirical evidence about the loss choice.
icml-2025-categorical-distributional-rei.tldr: A preconditioned categorical distributional RL algorithm gains convergence guarantees and an analysis of long-run variance when trained with KL divergence.

paragraphs: As generated content enters training datasets, later models increasingly learn from earlier models’ outputs. This paper investigates whether that process causes model collapse and how the answer depends on data management. It compares three training workflows across Gaussian estimation, kernel density estimation, and language-model finetuning.

Replacing all real data with successive generations of synthetic data produces collapse in every task setting studied. A different outcome appears when synthetic data accumulate alongside retained real data and each model trains on the entire collection. In those experiments, models remain stable and test losses do not diverge, even as the real-data share tends toward zero.

The third workflow accumulates real and synthetic data but trains each generation on a fixed-size subset. Here, test performance degrades slowly and gradually rather than explosively. These contrasting results indicate that synthetic content’s proportion alone does not determine the observed trajectory. Retaining data and deciding how much of the accumulated collection each generation actually uses are consequential parts of the training process.
icml-2025-collapse-or-thrive-perils-and-.tldr: Experiments show that replacing, accumulating, or subsampling synthetic training data leads to markedly different patterns of collapse, stability, or gradual degradation.

paragraphs: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning trains an agent to reach different goals using previously collected trajectories. Sparse rewards make this difficult. Reinterpreting intermediate states as goals supplies more learning examples, but this approach fails on goal-stitching tasks, where reaching a goal requires combining portions of different recorded trajectories.

Pairing states and goals across trajectories is a possible remedy, but the authors find that doing so directly can degrade performance. The problem is overestimating the value of state-goal pairs that are unconnected. Their method, Conservative Goal-Conditioned Implicit Value Learning, adds a penalty for these pairs and uses a quasimetric framework to estimate values for connected pairs.

This combination addresses both sides of the learning problem: discouraging unsupported high values while modeling connections that can support useful behavior. On OGBench, the authors report that the method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse tasks. The results support making cross-trajectory learning sensitive to connectivity, rather than assuming that arbitrary pairings provide equally reliable training targets.
icml-2025-conservative-offline-goal-cond.tldr: CGCIVL improves offline goal learning by penalizing unconnected state-goal pairs while modeling the values of connected pairs.

paragraphs: Data augmentation creates additional training examples to help models generalize. In classification, transformations can often preserve a class label, but augmentation for regression has received less attention. This paper develops a geometric approach to generating examples for tasks with numerical outputs, building on earlier work that approximates the structure of data locally.

The proposed Curvature-Enhanced Manifold Sampling method uses a second-order representation of the data manifold. A first-order approximation describes local directions; a second-order representation also captures curvature. The authors develop both a theoretical framework and practical tools for approximating and sampling general manifolds, then use this representation to sample and reconstruct new data points efficiently.

Across multiple datasets, the reported evaluations show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods, both within the training distribution and outside it. The added computational overhead is reported to be minimal. The contribution is therefore a way to make regression augmentation account for local bending in the data’s geometry, with empirical evidence that this richer approximation improves predictive performance.
icml-2025-curvature-enhanced-data-augmen.tldr: CEMS uses a second-order geometric representation to generate regression training data, improving reported performance with minimal computational overhead.

paragraphs: An image’s probability under a generative model does not necessarily track its perceived quality. The paper starts from findings that high-likelihood images tend to be smoother, while lower-likelihood images contain more detail. This makes control over sample density relevant to adjusting the balance between realism and visual detail.

The authors first analyze Prior Guidance, an existing method that changes detail by scaling the latent code. They introduce a condition called score alignment to explain its operation and show that this condition can be checked tractably for any continuous normalizing flow. This gives a testable explanation for when the existing technique’s behavior is supported.

They then propose Density Guidance, which modifies the differential equation governing generation to control log-density exactly during sampling. A stochastic extension retains precise density control while allowing controlled variation in structure or fine details. Experiments demonstrate fine-grained detail adjustments without sacrificing sample quality. Together, the analysis and method connect a statistical property of generated images to a controllable aspect of their appearance.
icml-2025-devil-is-in-the-details-densit.tldr: Density Guidance controls sampling log-density in flow models to adjust image detail, with experiments showing preserved sample quality.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects from observational data often relies on assuming that no relevant confounder went unmeasured. This paper develops a way to challenge that assumption when observations come from multiple heterogeneous environments. Its aim is falsification: detecting evidence against the assumption, rather than establishing that hidden confounding is absent.

The method builds on the observation that unmeasured confounding can make observed causal mechanisms appear dependent. The authors turn this into a two-stage procedure designed to detect such dependencies with high statistical power while controlling false positives. The approach uses differences across environments and does not require randomized experimental data.

A notable feature is that the procedure can still operate when environments directly affect the outcome, a violation of transportability that obstructs some other falsification approaches. Evaluations on simulated and semi-synthetic data demonstrate efficient confounding detection. The contribution is a statistical check on a consequential causal assumption in a multi-environment setting, including cases where outcome behavior cannot simply be treated as unchanged across sources.
icml-2025-falsification-of-unconfoundedn.tldr: A two-stage test uses dependencies across heterogeneous environments to detect evidence of hidden confounding without randomized data.

paragraphs: Predicting convincing motion does not by itself establish that a video model has learned physical laws. This paper tests whether diffusion-based video generators can extrapolate physical behavior from visual training data. The authors construct a two-dimensional simulation environment in which object movements and collisions follow one or more classical mechanics laws.

Models receive initial frames and predict subsequent motion. Scaling experiments distinguish examples within the training distribution, unfamiliar combinations, and examples outside the distribution. The authors report perfect generalization within the distribution and measurable scaling behavior for new combinations, but failure on out-of-distribution scenarios. Those differences separate successful prediction in familiar settings from broader physical extrapolation.

Further experiments suggest that the tested models generalize by imitating nearby training cases rather than extracting general physical rules. Their apparent priorities when choosing reference cases are color, then size, velocity, and shape. The findings suggest that scaling alone is insufficient for uncovering fundamental physical laws in these models, even when it produces strong performance on familiar forms of motion.
icml-2025-how-far-is-video-generation-fr.tldr: Controlled physics experiments suggest that scaled video generators imitate familiar cases but fail to extrapolate general physical laws.

paragraphs: An overparameterized model can represent many solutions, yet its training procedure may favor a simpler subset without an explicit simplicity penalty. This paper analyzes that implicit regularization in tensor factorization. It focuses on the tubal tensor product and its corresponding notion of low rank, motivated by the representation’s relevance to image data.

The central result establishes that gradient descent with a small random initialization favors solutions of low tubal rank in the studied overparameterized model. The analysis goes beyond the lazy training regime. It also treats discrete gradient-descent updates rather than gradient flow, the continuous-time formulation used in some earlier tensor results.

Numerical simulations illustrate the training dynamics predicted by the theory and emphasize the importance of keeping the random initialization small. The contribution extends rigorous understanding of optimization-induced simplicity from previously studied matrix settings into this tensor setting. Its guarantee is tied to the factorization model and initialization considered, making the starting scale a substantive part of the result rather than an incidental implementation choice.
icml-2025-implicit-regularization-for-tu.tldr: The paper proves that small random initialization makes gradient descent favor low-tubal-rank solutions in an overparameterized tensor factorization model.

paragraphs: Animal behavior outside tightly controlled tasks can reflect changing motivations that researchers cannot directly observe. Inverse reinforcement learning attempts to infer those motivations from actions. This paper argues that tracking changing rewards is insufficient when an animal’s choices also depend on its past decisions and environmental context.

The proposed SWIRL framework represents a long behavioral sequence as switches among shorter decision-making processes, each associated with a distinct reward function. It adds history dependence to both policies and rewards, allowing the model’s account of current behavior to incorporate past experience. The formulation is intended to capture biologically plausible influences of history while accommodating motivations that change over time.

The authors evaluate SWIRL on simulated and real animal behavior datasets. It outperforms models without history dependence in both quantitative and qualitative comparisons. These findings support including behavioral history when characterizing naturalistic decisions. The contribution is a framework that combines switching motivations and historical context, broadening the behaviors that an inverse-reinforcement-learning account can describe beyond short, repetitive tasks with explicit rewards.
icml-2025-inverse-reinforcement-learning.tldr: SWIRL combines changing rewards with history-dependent decisions to better characterize animal behavior in simulated and real datasets.

paragraphs: Many causal questions concern changing several variables together, even when available experiments changed only one variable at a time. This paper asks whether observational data and single-variable interventions can identify the effect of a joint intervention. Answering that question could make existing experimental evidence useful for combinations that were never directly tested.

The authors establish an identifiability result for a class of nonlinear additive outcome mechanisms. Within that class, joint effects can be inferred without joint-intervention data. They also propose a practical estimator that separates each intervention variable’s contribution into confounded and unconfounded parts, connecting the theoretical result to an implementable estimation procedure.

In synthetic experiments, the estimator performs comparably to models trained directly on joint-intervention data and better than an estimator relying only on observations. The result supports the value of combining observational and single-variable experimental evidence under the stated structural assumptions. Its reach is specifically tied to the analyzed additive mechanisms, rather than asserting that arbitrary joint interventions can always be reconstructed from separate experiments.
icml-2025-learning-joint-interventional-.tldr: For a class of nonlinear additive mechanisms, observational data and single-variable interventions suffice to identify joint intervention effects.

paragraphs: Past interaction data can speed up sequential decision-making, but users may differ in ways that are not directly observed. This paper studies linear contextual bandits in which each user has a high-dimensional reward parameter, while all users’ parameters lie in a shared low-dimensional subspace. The formulation accommodates uncountably many latent states.

An offline algorithm first learns this subspace with provable guarantees. Two online algorithms then use that estimate to accelerate learning. The first has a regret guarantee whose effective dimension decreases as the offline dataset grows, and a matching lower bound establishes minimax optimality. The second trades a slightly weaker guarantee for computational efficiency.

Experiments on synthetic data and MovieLens recommendations support the methods’ effectiveness. The authors also prove a de Finetti theorem for stateless decision processes to establish the broader generality of the latent-bandit model. The main practical connection is between shared structure learned from previous users and the cost of learning online: more offline evidence can make a high-dimensional problem behave like a lower-dimensional one.
icml-2025-leveraging-offline-data-in-lin.tldr: Learning a shared low-dimensional reward subspace from offline data enables faster online bandit learning with minimax-optimal regret guarantees.

paragraphs: A mixture-of-experts model uses a router to direct inputs toward specialized predictors. This paper investigates why that architecture can help gradient-based learning when a regression task contains hidden clusters. The analysis studies sample and runtime complexity under stochastic gradient descent for clusters governed by single-index models.

In the analyzed setting, an ordinary neural network fails to detect the latent organization and instead treats the task as a whole. The authors connect this difficulty to the information exponent: it is low within individual clusters but increases for the combined problem. The mixture-of-experts architecture can exploit the easier component tasks because individual experts can weakly recover the function associated with a cluster.

That initial recovery enables the model to divide the regression problem into more manageable subproblems. The contribution is a theoretical account of how specialization can emerge through training dynamics, rather than only an observation that a routed architecture performs well. Its conclusions concern the studied clustered nonlinear regression setting and explain an architectural advantage through the differing difficulty of learning components and their mixture.
icml-2025-mixture-of-experts-provably-de.tldr: A theoretical analysis shows how mixture-of-experts training can uncover hidden regression clusters that an ordinary network fails to separate in the studied setting.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents do not always observe the rewards associated with their actions. Human feedback can be unavailable, sensors can fail, and some rewards may remain inaccessible. Monitored Markov decision processes represent this distinction between what happens in the environment and which rewards a monitoring process reveals.

The paper introduces a model-based algorithm using two instances of interval estimation. One works to capture observable rewards reliably; the other learns a minimax-optimal policy. The design makes use of the problem’s structure and can exploit a known monitoring process. It also addresses limitations of earlier methods concerning initialization and settings where some rewards cannot be observed.

Across more than four dozen benchmarks, the method converges faster than prior algorithms, with larger improvements when the monitor is known. The authors additionally provide the first finite-sample performance bound for this setting and show convergence to a minimax-optimal policy even with permanently hidden rewards. This connects practical exploration improvements with guarantees that go beyond eventual, asymptotic convergence.
icml-2025-model-based-exploration-in-mon.tldr: A model-based exploration algorithm learns minimax-optimal policies with finite-sample guarantees even when some rewards are never observable.

paragraphs: Feature attribution seeks to identify which parts of an input influence a neural network’s decision. Pixel-level heatmaps offer a convenient visualization, but individual pixels do not adequately capture the underlying structure of images, audio representations, or volumes. This paper examines how changing the representation in which attribution is computed can produce more informative explanations.

The proposed Wavelet Attribution Method operates on wavelet coefficients, which localize information in both space and scale. These properties let explanations describe where influential information occurs and what scale of structure it involves. The approach supports inputs of any dimension, providing a common attribution framework across different types of data.

In quantitative evaluations across audio, images, and volumes, the method matches or exceeds existing gradient-based attribution methods. The authors also discuss connections between attribution, robustness, and transparency. The contribution is to make the attribution domain an explicit design choice: explaining a decision through spatially localized structures at multiple scales can reveal information that a pixel-based view fails to capture.
icml-2025-one-wave-to-explain-them-all-a.tldr: Wavelet-based attribution explains influential input structures by location and scale, matching or outperforming compared gradient-based methods across several modalities.

paragraphs: PokéChamp combines language models with minimax tree search for Pokémon battles. The language model supplies candidate player actions, models the opponent, and estimates position values. These roles let the search use gameplay history and human knowledge to narrow its choices and handle partially observed information, without additional language-model training.

In the Gen 9 OU format, the GPT-4o version wins 76% of games against the strongest existing language-model bot and 84% against the strongest rule-based bot. Using an eight-billion-parameter Llama 3.1 model, it wins 64% against the previous leading GPT-4o-powered bot. Its projected ladder Elo is 1300–1500, corresponding to the top 30%–10% of human players.

The work also assembles more than three million real-player games, including over 500,000 high-Elo matches, and builds skill benchmarks and puzzles from them. Alongside game-engine updates, these resources support evaluating particular battle abilities. The overall contribution shows how language-model judgments can support game-theoretic search in a competitive setting requiring decisions under incomplete information.
icml-2025-pokechamp-an-expert-level-mini.tldr: PokéChamp integrates language-model judgments into minimax search and outperforms leading Pokémon bots without additional LLM training.

paragraphs: A language model can become less useful when its safety behavior causes it to reject benign requests. This paper studies how the amount and type of teacher-generated finetuning data affect that balance. It examines generating additional completions for both general-purpose and toxic prompts using an advanced teacher model.

Overgenerating completions for general-purpose prompts substantially improves safety while having only a minimal effect on usefulness. The reported F1 measure combining safety and usefulness rises from 74.4% to 91.8%. Overgeneration for toxic prompts raises usefulness from 11.1% to 57.6% while preserving safety, showing different effects from expanding these two categories of training material.

The authors also introduce POROver for models that are already highly safe but refuse too often. It uses preference optimization with teacher-model completions to reduce unnecessary refusals. Applying it increases usefulness further, from 57.6% to 82.1%, with comparable safety. The reported results show how data generation and subsequent preference training can improve the safety-usefulness balance in the evaluated models.
icml-2025-porover-improving-safety-and-r.tldr: Teacher-generated completions and POROver preference optimization improve reported usefulness while maintaining strong safety and reducing unnecessary refusals.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders are used to interpret language-model activations, but their progress is often measured with indirect, unsupervised metrics. This paper introduces SAEBench to examine whether improvements on those proxies correspond to better interpretability and practical usefulness. Its eight metrics cover interpretation, separation of features, and applications such as unlearning.

The authors release more than 200 sparse autoencoders spanning seven architectures and training algorithms, enabling systematic comparisons. Their evaluation finds that better proxy scores do not reliably imply better practical performance. For example, Matryoshka autoencoders score slightly worse on existing proxies but substantially better on feature disentanglement, with that advantage increasing as the autoencoders scale.

The benchmark makes these differences visible within a standardized evaluation framework. An interactive interface also supports exploring relationships among metrics across the released models. The contribution is a richer basis for judging architectural and training changes: a method’s strengths can vary by the property being measured, and scaling trends may look different when evaluation moves beyond the usual proxy objectives.
icml-2025-saebench-a-comprehensive-bench.tldr: SAEBench evaluates sparse autoencoders across eight metrics and shows that proxy improvements do not reliably predict practical gains.

paragraphs: This paper compares learning a parametric model through gradient updates with learning a linear combination of random features. Its focus is distribution-free learning, where the learning guarantee makes no assumptions about the data distribution. The authors ask how much additional expressive learning power gradient-based training provides under that demanding requirement.

Their main theorem is conditional: if mini-batch stochastic gradient descent can learn the parametric model distribution-free, then random features can approximate the target with high probability using a polynomial-sized combination. The required size depends on the number of gradient steps and their numerical precision. This connects the resources used by optimization to those needed by a random-feature representation.

The authors also introduce average probabilistic dimension complexity, prove a polynomial relationship with statistical query dimension, and establish an infinite separation from standard dimension complexity. Together, these results characterize limits of distribution-free gradient learning. They help explain why assumptions about data distributions can be consequential when seeking advantages from neural-network training beyond what random-feature combinations can already represent.
icml-2025-the-power-of-random-features-a.tldr: Anything learnable distribution-free by the analyzed mini-batch gradient method can also be approximated with polynomially many random features, with high probability.

paragraphs: At very low bitrates, image compression must coordinate the information it stores with the generative model used to reconstruct the image. This paper identifies fragmented integration of semantic retrieval, latent compression, and generation as a source of poor fidelity and coding efficiency. ResULIC connects these components through residual information.

Its Semantic Residual Coding component captures the semantic difference between the original image and its compressed latent representation. Residual signals inform both semantic retrieval and diffusion-based generation, while a perceptual fidelity optimizer improves reconstruction quality. A Compression-aware Diffusion Model additionally aligns bitrate with diffusion time steps, coordinating the reconstruction procedure with the amount of encoded information.

The reported experiments show better objective and subjective performance than the compared state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods. The authors report BD-rate reductions of 80.7% for LPIPS and 66.3% for FID. These findings support the proposed integration: encoding what the compressed representation misses and adapting generation to compression conditions can improve the measured relationship between bitrate and reconstructed image quality.
icml-2025-ultra-lowrate-image-compressio.tldr: ResULIC combines semantic residual coding with bitrate-aware diffusion to improve image reconstruction and coding efficiency at ultra-low rates.

paragraphs: When a language model receives a reward only after a multistep solution, training must determine which earlier steps deserve credit. PPO commonly uses a value network to estimate future return for this purpose. This paper investigates whether those estimates adequately distinguish useful reasoning steps from less useful alternatives.

The authors find substantial shortcomings on reasoning-heavy tasks: value networks often estimate expected return poorly and barely exceed a random baseline when comparing alternative steps. They propose VinePPO, which uses the flexibility of language environments to obtain unbiased estimates through Monte Carlo sampling. The method changes the evidence used for credit assignment rather than relying on the problematic value estimates.

Across MATH and GSM8K, VinePPO consistently outperforms PPO and other baselines while requiring less wall-clock time, with speedups reaching 3.0 times. It also achieves higher test accuracy at a given training accuracy. That relationship suggests the improved results involve stronger generalization per sample, supporting accurate credit assignment as a meaningful component of reinforcement learning for language-model reasoning.
icml-2025-vineppo-refining-credit-assign.tldr: VinePPO replaces unreliable value-network credit estimates with unbiased Monte Carlo estimates, improving mathematical reasoning results and training time in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: A model can learn to reproduce training solutions without becoming equally reliable on unfamiliar problems. This paper studies that distinction during mathematical finetuning by separating correct final answers from exact copying of training reasoning steps. It introduces pre-memorization train accuracy: accuracy on training queries before generated solutions begin replicating those steps.

Across Llama3 8B, Gemma2 9B, GSM8k, MATH, and varied training configurations, this metric predicts dataset-level test accuracy with an R-squared of at least 0.9. At the individual-example level, it also indicates whether predictions remain robust when a training query is perturbed. The findings connect when correctness emerges during learning with how well that correctness transfers.

The authors then use the metric to guide data selection. Prioritizing examples with low pre-memorization accuracy yields reported data-efficiency improvements of 1.5 to 2 times over independent, identically distributed scaling and other scaling techniques. This makes the learning-dynamics measurement practically useful: it can identify training examples worth prioritizing, while distinguishing early solution success from later replication of supplied reasoning.
icml-2025-what-do-learning-dynamics-reve.tldr: Accuracy before a model starts copying training reasoning strongly predicts test performance and guides more data-efficient mathematical finetuning.

paragraphs: Crystal symmetry influences properties including conductivity, optical behavior, and mechanical strength. Generative models that inadequately represent symmetry can struggle to produce structures that are both stable and symmetrically valid. This paper introduces WyFormer, which explicitly conditions generation on space group symmetry and represents crystal structure through Wyckoff positions.

The resulting representation is discrete and compressed, making symmetry part of how structures are described. To learn its distribution, the authors construct an autoregressive model based on a Transformer encoder without positional encoding. The model is permutation invariant, so its treatment of the representation does not depend on an arbitrary ordering of its elements.

Experiments report best-in-class symmetry-conditioned generation alongside competitive structural stability and material-property prediction accuracy, including prediction without atomic coordinates. The authors also report unmatched inference speed in their evaluations. The contribution combines a physics-motivated representation with a suitable generative architecture, showing that explicit symmetry structure can support generation, property prediction, and efficient inference within the same modeling approach.
icml-2025-wyckoff-transformer-generation.tldr: WyFormer uses a compact symmetry-based crystal representation to support strong symmetry-conditioned generation, competitive property prediction, and fast inference.
